source: Static Friction
Static friction matches the push up to a limit of μ_s N; beyond that, the object slides.
Students always set static friction equal to μ_s N, even when the object is far from slipping.
Push gently on a heavy dresser and it doesn't move. Something matches your push exactly: static friction, the grip between surfaces that aren't sliding. Unlike Kinetic Friction, it has no fixed size.

Static friction is as large as it needs to be to prevent sliding, up to a limit: $f_s \le \mu_s F_N$. Below the limit, find $f_s$ from the balance of forces; past the limit, the object starts to slide and kinetic friction takes over.

At rest, the net force is zero, so friction must cancel whatever else pushes along the surface. Push with $50\ \text{N}$ and friction gives $50\ \text{N}$; push with $80\ \text{N}$ and it gives $80\ \text{N}$, until the bumps between the surfaces can't hold any more. Usually $\mu_s > \mu_k$, which is why a stuck object lurches once it breaks free.
A 20 kg box with μ_s = 0.5: static friction can hold up to 98 N.
Worked examples
A $30\ \text{kg}$ crate rests on a floor with $\mu_s = 0.5$. You push with $60\ \text{N}$ and it doesn't move. How big is the static friction?
Less than the limit
At rest: friction balances the push, so $f_s = 60\ \text{N}$.
The limit, $\mu_s F_N = 0.5 \times 294 = 147\ \text{N}$, is not reached.
What is the smallest push that starts that crate sliding? If $\mu_k = 0.35$ and you keep pushing with that force, what is its acceleration?
Breaking loose
$147\ \text{N}$; then about $1.47\ \text{m/s}^2$
Limit: $\mu_s mg = 147\ \text{N}$. A push just above that starts it moving.
Sliding: $f_k = 0.35 \times 294 \approx 103\ \text{N}$, so $a \approx \dfrac{147 - 103}{30} \approx 1.47\ \text{m/s}^2$.

Always setting static friction equal to $\mu_s N$, even when the object is far from slipping. $\mu_s N$ is a maximum, like the weight limit on a shelf, not the actual force. Check: if the object stays at rest, get $f_s$ from $\Sigma F = 0$; use $\mu_s N$ only to test whether it can hold.
